newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea says arrests U.S. spy, tensions rise.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea says arrests U.S. spy, tensions rise.

text.p: North Korea said on Sunday it had arrested a U.S. citizen spying for South Korea, dragging Washington further into escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula.
A South Korean security official dismissed the charge as a fabrication, while the U.S. embassy in Seoul could not confirm any details about the alleged agent.
The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said Evan Carl Hunzike was arrested on August 24 by a North Korean security organisation after he crossed the Amnok River on the Chinese border into North Korea.
KCNA did not identify him further or explain why he had been held since late August.

"He admitted that he is a U.S. citizen and that he illegally entered the DPRK (Democratic People's Republic of Korea) for the purpose of getting information on its domestic situation," the communique said.

"It has been proved by investigation that he was sent for espionage by South Korea's Agency for National Security Planning. He will have to take appropriate penal responsibility under the DPRK criminal law."
A spokesman at the U.S. embassy in Seoul said: "We're trying to determine if he's a U.S. citizen. As far as I'm aware, this hasn't been determined yet."
A spokesman for South Korea's Agency for National Security Planning said: "We've never heard of the name. The allegation was made up by the North."
The charge drags Washington deeper into an angry feud between North and South Korea over the deaths of 22 of 26 North Koreans who landed by submarine in the South last month.
Pyongyang has demanded the return of the vessel along with the survivors and the bodies of the dead crew.
In a separate KCNA statement on Sunday, Pyongyang accused Seoul of trying to spark a war.
"Today when the Cold War has ended, their frantic arms buildup is only intended to provoke a war against the north," KCNA quoted a commentary in the official Rodong Sinmun newspaper as saying.
"Their reckless confrontation and war moves against the DPRK will only precipitate their doom," it said.
South Korea's 655,000 troops, bolstered by about 37,000 U.S. forces, face the North's 1.1 million-strong army. A ceasefire accord has preserved the peace since the 1950-53 Korean War.
On Saturday, North Korea warned of "merciless retaliation" and vowed "blood for blood" in a KCNA communique that also raised espionage charges against Washington.

Although Washington has condemned the submarine incursion as a violation of the ceasefire agreement, the only active U.S. role in the drama so far has been helping in the hunt for fugitive North Koreans from the vessel.
Analysts said the spy charges appeared to be part of efforts by Pyongyang to divert attention from the submarine incident by creating a new crisis.
North Korea is constantly seeking ways to drive a wedge between Washington and Seoul and engage the United States in direct negotiations.
A crisis over North Korea's suspected nuclear weapons programme was defused by a 1994 U.S.-North Korean deal.

In response to Pyongyang's threats, Seoul has stepped up security at airports, ports and diplomatic missions, assigned more bodyguards to key public figures and tightened vigilance on five west coast islands seen vulnerable to attack.
On Saturday, Seoul's Foreign Ministry warned South Korean travellers to watch out for North Korean terrorism, especially in China and Russia.
"We recommended travel agencies refrain from sending travellers to the northeastern provinces of China and the Far Eastern region of Russia," the ministry said in a statement.
The brutal murder of a South Korean diplomat in the Russian Far East city of Vladivostok last Tuesday sparked fears that the North had begun to make good on its retaliation threats.
Pyongyang has denied involvement in the murder.
Local media reported on Sunday that Seoul would freeze all economic cooperation with the North until ties improved.
